factOrAssumption.scenario: John was late for school this morning.
factOrAssumption.statement: He was late because it was raining hard.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: we know he was late, but we don't know why yet. It could be the rain, or it could be something else.

factOrAssumption.scenario: The classroom clock shows 8 o'clock and John walked in at 8:15.
factOrAssumption.statement: John walked in 15 minutes after 8 o'clock.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is a fact: we can check it just by looking at the time, without imagining anything.

factOrAssumption.scenario: A plant on the classroom windowsill is taller than it was a week ago.
factOrAssumption.statement: The plant grew because someone watered it every day.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: we know it grew, but we don't yet know the exact cause — it could be the water, the light, or something else.

factOrAssumption.scenario: You measured the plant on Monday and it was 12 cm. Today it measures 15 cm.
factOrAssumption.statement: The plant grew 3 cm this week.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is a fact: it's the result of a measurement anyone could repeat and confirm.

factOrAssumption.scenario: Your friend didn't reply to your message today.
factOrAssumption.statement: She must be angry with you.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: there could be many reasons — maybe she's busy, without a phone, or asleep. You don't know yet.

factOrAssumption.scenario: The sky is full of dark clouds.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is a reasonable assumption, but it's not certain yet — dark clouds don't always bring rain.

factOrAssumption.scenario: Tom fell off the swing at the playground and his knee turned red.
factOrAssumption.statement: He fell because he was swinging too fast.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: we know he fell, but we don't know the exact reason — it could be speed, or something else.

factOrAssumption.scenario: A burnt smell was noticed in the kitchen after lunch.
factOrAssumption.statement: The toast burned because the toaster was left on too long.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: we know something burned, but we don't yet know for sure what caused it.

factOrAssumption.scenario: Rita's dog barked all night long.
factOrAssumption.statement: The dog barked because it saw a cat in the garden.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: there could be many reasons the dog barked — we don't know for sure it was a cat.

factOrAssumption.scenario: You weighed your backpack yesterday and it was 3 kg. Today it weighs 4 kg.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is a fact: it's the direct result of weighing it, something anyone can check.

factOrAssumption.scenario: The flowers in the school garden are wilted this week.
factOrAssumption.statement: The flowers wilted because nobody watered them.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is an assumption: the flowers could have wilted for other reasons too, like heat or pests — we don't know for sure yet.

factOrAssumption.scenario: Your report card shows you got 18 out of 20 on the maths test.
factOrAssumption.statement: You got 18 out of 20 on the test.
factOrAssumption.explanation: This is a fact: it's written on the report card and anyone can check it.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You left an ice cream in the sun for half an hour, and when you came back it had melted.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: The sun's heat melts ice — there is a direct, well-known link between heat and melting.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: Whenever Maria wears her blue jumper, her football team wins the game.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: A jumper can't influence the result of a game. It's just coincidence — it happened to line up a few times by chance.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You stopped watering a cactus for a month and it started to wilt.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: Plants need water to live. Missing water directly explains why the cactus wilted.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: On the day you wore yellow socks, you got a good grade on your test.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: The colour of your socks has no connection to a test result. It's just coincidence.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You ate lots of sweets this week and now you have a toothache.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: Sugar helps create cavities, which cause toothaches — there is a known link between the two.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: Whenever you bring your umbrella, it doesn't rain; when you forget it at home, it rains.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: Bringing or forgetting an umbrella doesn't influence the weather. We just notice these coincidences more than the times they don't happen.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You slept only a few hours last night and today you feel tired and low on energy in class.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: The body needs sleep to recover energy. Sleeping too little directly causes tiredness the next day.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: Whenever you pick the number 7 in a raffle, you feel like you're going to win — and sometimes you do.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: The number you pick doesn't influence a random raffle draw. It's coincidence: with enough tries, winning sometimes was bound to happen.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You put on sunscreen before going to the beach and didn't get sunburnt.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: Sunscreen blocks the rays that burn skin — there is a direct, well-established link between the two.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: Whenever you wear your red cap, your basketball team wins the game.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: A cap can't influence the result of a basketball game played by other people. It's just coincidence.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: You rode your bike every day this week and your legs feel stronger.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: Regular exercise strengthens muscles — this is a known effect explained by science.

causeOrCoincidence.scenario: Grandma says the dog gets more restless on full-moon nights.
causeOrCoincidence.explanation: There's no scientific proof that the full moon affects dogs' behaviour. It's probably coincidence or just a popular belief.

missingInfo.scenario: Two identical plants were planted on the same day. One grew well, the other barely grew at all.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most to figure out what happened?

options.text: ☀️ Did both plants get the same amount of light?
🎨 What colour is each plant's pot?
📅 What day of the week was each one planted?

missingInfo.afterNote: You could also ask about water or temperature — the important thing is looking for what's different between the two plants.

missingInfo.scenario: The school bus didn't arrive at its usual time this morning.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most to find out why?

options.text: 🚦 Was there heavy traffic or a problem on the road?
🎒 What colour is your backpack today?
🍎 What did you have for breakfast?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about traffic, a breakdown, or the route helps you get closer to the real cause.

missingInfo.scenario: The classroom's pet fish was found floating belly-up this morning.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most to understand what happened?

options.text: 🌡️ Did the tank's water change temperature or cleanliness?
🖍️ Who drew the fish tank on the classroom wall?
📖 How many pages does the book about fish have?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about the water, the food, or how long this has been going on helps you find useful clues.

missingInfo.scenario: The cake grandma baked today didn't rise in the oven like it usually does.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most to figure out why?

options.text: 🧁 Were the same ingredients and amounts used as usual?
🎵 What music was playing in the kitchen?
🧦 What colour were grandma's socks?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about the ingredients, the oven temperature, or the baking time are good clues to investigate.

missingInfo.scenario: The school team lost yesterday's game, after winning the three games before it.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most understand what was different?

options.text: 🩹 Was an important player injured or missing from the game?
🌈 What colour was the sky during the game?
🕐 What time did the players wake up three days earlier?

missingInfo.afterNote: Comparing what changed from one game to the next — players, opponent, tiredness — helps you find explanations.

missingInfo.scenario: Mum's phone was charged to 100% last night and this morning it only had 20%.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most find out why?

options.text: 📲 Were apps running all night in the background?
🎨 What colour is the phone case?
📏 How big is the phone?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about open apps, screen brightness, or battery age helps you understand what used up the energy.

missingInfo.scenario: Rui's bike tyre was nice and full yesterday and today it's completely flat.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most find the reason?

options.text: 🔍 Is there a hole or a sharp object stuck in the tyre?
🎨 What colour is the bike seat?
📆 What year was the bike bought?

missingInfo.afterNote: Checking for a puncture, a loose valve, or an improperly closed tyre helps you find the real cause.

missingInfo.scenario: Two siblings played together outside all day. One caught a cold the next day and the other didn't.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most understand the difference?

options.text: 🧣 Did one of them spend more time in the cold or get wet?
👟 What shoes did they wear while playing?
📺 What show did they watch on TV that evening?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about clothing, time spent in the cold, or contact with someone already sick helps you investigate the cause.

missingInfo.scenario: In the school garden, the tomatoes in one bed grew a lot and the ones in another bed barely grew at all.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most find out why?

options.text: 💧 Do both beds get the same amount of water and sun?
🪧 What names do the garden beds have?
🕰️ What time do lessons start?

missingInfo.afterNote: Comparing water, light, and soil type between the two beds helps you see what's different.

missingInfo.scenario: The teacher heard noise in the classroom when she stepped out for a minute, but no one wants to say what happened.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most find out the truth?

options.text: 👀 Did anyone see what happened right before the noise started?
📏 How many desks are in the classroom?
🖍️ What colour is the whiteboard?

missingInfo.afterNote: Calmly asking witnesses what they saw, without blaming anyone right away, helps you get closer to the truth.

missingInfo.scenario: Your little brother's favourite toy has disappeared from his room.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most find it?

options.text: 🕵️ Where was the last place anyone remembers seeing it?
🎈 What colour was the toy?
📅 What month was he born in?

missingInfo.afterNote: Remembering the last place it was seen and searching nearby is usually the best place to start.

missingInfo.scenario: Two children in the class missed school this week, both with a fever.
missingInfo.question: Which of these questions would help you most see if it's connected?

options.text: 🤝 Were they close to each other, or to someone already sick, before falling ill?
🎒 What brand is their backpack?
🔤 What letter does their name start with?

missingInfo.afterNote: Asking about recent contact helps you understand whether an illness is spreading among classmates.

contradictions.statementA: Ana's cat is completely black, with no other colour at all.
contradictions.statementB: Ana's cat has a white patch on its paw.
contradictions.explanation: If the cat is completely black, it can't also have a white patch — both statements can't be true at the same time.

contradictions.statementB: Pedro is younger than his sister, who is 10.
contradictions.explanation: There's no contradiction: it's perfectly possible to be 8 and have an older sister who is 10.

contradictions.statementA: Not a single drop of rain fell all day.
contradictions.statementB: The streets were soaked with water by the afternoon.
contradictions.explanation: If it didn't rain at all, it's strange for the streets to be soaked — unless there's another explanation, the statements contradict each other.

contradictions.statementB: I still haven't finished it, I'm only on page 80.
contradictions.explanation: There's no contradiction: a book can have 120 pages while someone is still halfway through, on page 80.

contradictions.statementA: Sofia was the first to reach the finish line of the race.
contradictions.statementB: Three classmates reached the finish line before Sofia.
contradictions.explanation: If Sofia was first, no one could have arrived before her — the two statements can't both be true.

contradictions.statementB: In sunlight, Miguel's jumper looks almost black.
contradictions.explanation: There's no contradiction: a very dark blue can indeed look almost black in certain light.

contradictions.statementA: David is the tallest student in the whole class.
contradictions.statementB: David is shorter than Beatriz, who is in his class.
contradictions.explanation: If David is the tallest in the class, no one in the class can be taller than him — both statements can't be true.

contradictions.statementA: The shop opens at 9am and always closes at 6pm.
contradictions.statementB: We went to the shop at 7pm and it was still open.
contradictions.explanation: If the shop always closes at 6pm, it couldn't be open at 7pm — unless there was an exception, the statements contradict each other.

contradictions.statementB: In sunlight, Marco's eyes look almost golden.
contradictions.explanation: There's no contradiction: a light brown can shine with a golden tone under strong light.

contradictions.statementA: No student in the class ran the 100 metres in under 20 seconds.
contradictions.statementB: Carla, who is in that class, ran the 100 metres in 18 seconds.
contradictions.explanation: If Carla is in the class and ran it in 18 seconds, then at least one student ran under 20 seconds — the statements can't both be true.

contradictions.statementA: It was a perfectly sunny day in the morning, without a single cloud in the sky.
contradictions.statementB: At night, thunder was heard and a lightning bolt was seen.
contradictions.explanation: There's no contradiction: the weather can change throughout the day — starting sunny and ending in a thunderstorm is perfectly normal.

contradictions.statementA: Tiago's piggy bank had 20 euros in it on Friday.
contradictions.statementB: On Saturday, with no one putting money in or taking any out, the piggy bank had 35 euros.
contradictions.explanation: If no one touched the piggy bank, the money couldn't have increased on its own — the two statements can't both be true.
